documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                         BEFORE THE
                           FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


           PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al.,              Docket Nos. EL25-49-000
                                                                         EL25-49-002



               Large Loads Co-Located at                                  AD24-11-001
               Generating Facilities


             Constellation Energy Generation
                      L.L.C.                                               EL25-20-001
                                                                           (consolidated)
                             v.

               PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.

                                                                           ER26-1479-000
               PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.


         REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OR, IN THE ALTERNATIVE, REHEARING
     OF EOLIAN, L.P., CALIBRANT ENERGY HOLDINGS, LLC, AND VERRUS, LLC

         Pursuant to section 313(a) of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”), 16 U.S.C. § 825l (2024),

and Rule 713 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy Regulatory

Commission (“Commission” or “FERC”),1 Eolian, L.P. (“Eolian”), Calibrant Energy Holdings,

LLC (“Calibrant”), and Verrus, LLC request clarification, and the in alterative rehearing of the

Commission’s June 18 Order in the above-captioned proceeding (Order). In brief, we seek

clarification of two aspects of the Order concerning the new Interim Network Integration

Transmission Service (“Interim NITS”). First, the Commission should clarify that PJM's tariff

must generally describe the reliability principles and circumstances under which these services

may be curtailed, and not merely their relative curtailment priority. Second, the Commission


1
    18 C.F.R. § 385.713.

                                                    1
 should clarify that a transmission customer taking Interim NITS may rely on any resource whose

capacity is not committed to be delivered to PJM or another entity during curtailment events.

                        LIST OF ERRORS/STATEMENT OF ISSUES

       We seek clarification or rehearing on two issues:

       1.      The Commission should clarify that, in providing details on the curtailment
               priority of Interim NITS, non-firm and firm contract demand service vis-à-vis
               existing transmission services, PJM must specify at least the general reliability
               circumstances under which curtailment may occur.

               a.     Failure to provide clarity on these service terms fails to adequately specify
                      tariff terms as required by the Federal Power Act. See 16 U.S.C. §
                      824d(c); City of Cleveland v. FERC, 773 F.2d 1368, 1376 (D.C. Cir.
                      1985); Hecate Energy Greene County 3 LLC v. FERC, 72 F.4th 1307, 1314
                      (D.C. Cir. 2023).

               b.     Lack of specificity in curtailment terms is unjust and unreasonable
                      because it will make use of these services commercially unworkable and
                      therefore will not adequately enable the avoidance of costly and inefficient
                      transmission system buildout that may not be necessary. See 16 U.S.C. §
                      824d(a); PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 (2025).

               c.     Lack of specificity in curtailment terms risks undue discrimination as
                      between transmission customers in application. See 16 U.S.C § 824d(a);
                      E.ON Climate & Renewables N. Am., LLC, 137 FERC ¶ 61,076, at P 38
                      (2011); Standardization of Generator Interconnection Agreements and
                      Procedures, Order No. 2003, 104 FERC ¶ 61,103, at P 11 (2003).




                                                    2
          2.      The Commission should clarify that any resource that has not committed its
                 capacity to PJM or another entity may be relied upon by a transmission customer
                 taking Interim NITS during curtailment events to the extent it is capable of
                 delivering capacity to the customer.

                 a.     Prohibiting such resources from offering their services to Interim NITS
                        customers during curtailment events would not be just and reasonable
                        because it would prevent efficient use of Interim NITS and unreasonably
                        deny resources the opportunity to sell their services. See 16 U.S.C. §
                        824d(a); PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 (2025);
                        Electric Storage Participation in Markets Operated by Regional
                        Transmission Organizations and Independent System Operators, Order
                        No. 841, 162 FERC ¶ 61,127 (2018).

                 b.     Prohibiting such resources from offering their services to Interim NITS
                        customers during curtailment events would be unduly discriminatory
                        because all resources whose services are not committed to PJM or another
                        entity are similarly situated to the two specific classes of resources the
                        Commission requires PJM to allow Interim NITS customers to rely upon.
                        See 16 U.S.C. § 824d(b); Associated Gas Distributors v. FERC, 824 F.2d
                        981, 998 (D.C. Cir. 1987); Consol. Edison Co. of N.Y. v. FERC, 45 F.4th
                        265, 281 (D.C. Cir. 2022); El Paso Natural Gas Co. Aera Energy, L.L.C.,
                        104 FERC ¶ 61,045, at P 115 (2003); N.Y. Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 162
                        FERC ¶ 61,124, at P 10 (2018).

         To the extent that the requested clarifications are denied, we respectfully request

rehearing.

II.      The Commission Should Clarify that PJM Must Describe the General Reliability
         Circumstances Pursuant to Which Interim NITS, Non-Firm and Firm Contract
         Demand Services May Each Be Curtailed.

         The June 18 Order “disagree[s] with commenters that PJM must provide specific details

in its Tariff, such as the trigger and procedures for curtailment of Interim NITS and FCD or

NFCD transmission services, or how PJM will enforce its curtailment procedures.”2 It finds that

“requiring PJM to specify the curtailment priority of [the] new transmission services in its Tariff,

while leaving specific implementation details in its manuals and individual service agreements,

provides transmission customers sufficient certainty as to their priority relative to other


2
    Order at P 552.

                                                      3
 transmission services and ensures that PJM has sufficient flexibility to preserve system reliability

in varying operating conditions.”3

       As a general matter, Eolian believes that a unified, specific approach to reliability triggers

for non-firm service adopted across grid operators and based on existing reliability frameworks

would provide clear and consistent rules of the road to developers of load and generation

resources, thereby reducing transaction costs, and facilitating the scale-up of efficient, cost-

effective business models for the development of load and supply designed to take advantage of

non-firm service. And by basing such triggers on transparent, actionable, and already-established

reliability criteria—such as limiting resource adequacy-based curtailment to NERC energy

emergency alert thresholds of EOP-011, and limiting transmission security-based curtailment

based on market-based dispatch of a dispatchable load bidding at the cap—a clear and consistent

trigger across regions would provide grid operators controls within the existing reliability

framework and procedures that ensure adequate system reliability.4 And by basing such triggers

on the existing reliability framework and procedures, regions can avoid needless disputes about

application of business practices. While we urge the Commission to consider providing all

regions with direction or other encouragement to adopt such criteria, we recognize that this

proceeding may not be the appropriate place for the Commission to establish such a specific,

nationwide rule.




3
  Id.
4
  See Attachment A, Affidavit of Andrew Levitt on Behalf of Eolian, L.P. (July 17, 2026) (“Levitt
Affidavit”) (explaining the benefits of a clear standard, and reasons to set the curtailment trigger
for resource adequacy events at EEA2 and for transmission security events based on market-
based dispatch of a dispatchable load as a suitable trigger for transmission security, with a cap on
bid prices (e.g., $3,700/MWh, as for certain demand response in PJM today)).

                                                      4
         Nonetheless, we request clarification, or in the alternative, rehearing, of the

Commission’s findings because while “specific details” regarding the curtailment trigger may be

appropriately included in the business practices manuals, Commission precedent and case law

interpreting the Federal Power Act make clear that the tariff must at least describe generally

when curtailment will occur. Moreover, including such general circumstances in the tariff will

help avoid commercial uncertainty that risks undermining the Commission’s objectives in

requiring PJM to establish these new transmission services in the first place.

        PJM must at minimum provide tariff language that not only specifies curtailment priority

order but also explains the reliability circumstances when curtailment may occur. PJM’s proposal

has not cleared that low bar. The Commission should provide further guidance to PJM, which

would set the stage for PJM to follow up with manual language establishing workable specific

implementation details that enable commercial investments while ensuring reliable system

operations.5 Providing the general boundaries for curtailment would be consistent with PJM’s

tariff terms for other types of transmission service.6 Far from compromising system operations,

providing more guidance on curtailment triggers will ameliorate potential challenges to dispatch

coordination.7 PJM’s far more detailed tariff provisions on curtailment for products such as

demand response help support investments into such resources, which enhances system

reliability.8 More specificity regarding when transmission services may be curtailed would do the

same.



5
  As Andrew Levitt describes in affidavit attached hereto as Attachment A, a reasonable
standard—though not necessarily the only reasonable standard—would establish that non-firm
NITS and non-firm contract demand service may be curtailed when specific resource adequacy
or transmission security triggers occur. Levitt Affidavit at 7-11.
6
  Id. at 5-6.
7
  Id.
8
  Id.

                                                      5
        As described in the attached affidavit of Andrew Levitt, PJM’s proposal does not set any

limit on the circumstances in which it may curtail customers taking the new transmission

services, because while it provides that such customers will be curtailed before pre-emergency

demand response, it provides no condition after which such curtailment will be called.9 As

explained in the Joint Co-Location Developers Reply Brief, “[t]his open-ended process . . .

theoretically allows PJM to curtail such services at any time.”10 Without any boundary limiting

the conditions under which curtailment may occur (e.g. limiting curtailment to certain defined

reliability circumstances), the tariff proposal fails to provide adequate notice of its service terms.

The Commission’s Order requires PJM to provide greater specificity insofar as PJM must amend

its proposal to provide for the relative curtailment priority of these new transmission services and

PJM’s existing services. Depending on how PJM responds, however, this may not necessarily

guarantee that PJM will book-end its proposal to provide a clear boundary beyond which

curtailment will not occur. For example, if PJM provides that curtailment of non-firm contract

demand service may occur prior to curtailment of other services, then the outer boundary of

when curtailment may occur would remain entirely undefined. In particular, to the extent that

PJM indicates that the new services may be curtailed prior to non-firm point-to-point service, or

in circumstances that differ from point-to-point service, then such a response to the

Commission’s directive would fail to provide market participants with any clear limits on or

ability to forecast when curtailment may be called. It is not clear that the Commission



9
  Id. at 4. PJM’s proposed tariff provisions specified that PJM “may curtail Interim Network
Integration Transmission Service prior to dispatching the Pre-Emergency Load Response
Program as further set forth in the PJM Manuals, or in response to a transfer capability shortage
as a result of system reliability conditions.” PJM Initial Brief, Illustrative Tariff, Part XI, Subpart
B, § 705.2 & Subpart C, § 713.4.
10
   Reply Brief of Joint Co-location Developers and Motion to Intervene Out-of-time of Calibrant,
Convergent, U.S. Energy Storage Coalition, and Verrus, at 17 (filed Mar. 25, 2026).

                                                      6
 contemplated this circumstance and intended such open-ended levels of curtailment. As such, the

Commission should clarify its order by directing PJM to include general principles and

conditions where curtailment may occur when using Interim NITS. PJM could then provide

additional specificity in its manuals.

        Under City of Cleveland v. FERC and the Commission’s “rule of reason” precedent, a

tariff must include “practices that affect rates and service significantly, that are realistically

susceptible of specification, and that are not so generally understood in any contractual

arrangement as to render recitation superfluous.”11 While it is true that tariffs “need not include

mere implementation details,”12 the general circumstances when curtailment may occur are core

to the definition of the new transmission services. As Levitt states, the “curtailment trigger is not

a minor feature of the new FERC-required transmission services, but one of the key attributes

that determines the value of the service and the associated impacts of the new large load on the

balance of transmission customers.”13 Decisions whether to take such services hinge on the

ability to estimate the depth and length of potential curtailments, and to plan for such

curtailments, such as assessing the extent to which investments in on-site resources or other

measures would allow the load to withstand such curtailments.14 As developers of generation,



11
   773 F.2d 1368, 1376 (D.C. Cir. 1985) (emphasis in original).
12
   Hecate Energy Greene County 3 LLC v. FERC, 72 F.4th 1307, 1312 (D.C. Cir. 2023)
13
   Levitt Affidavit at 4.
14
   See id. (“The difference between a service curtailed only during defined emergency conditions
and one curtailed based on broad operational discretion is not small, and will directly impact the
investment feasibility, characteristics, and impact of each of these services.”). For example, in
assessing the potential for energy storage resources located at the point of interconnection to
support a transmission customer’s ability to take one of the new transmission services, a
developer may assess whether a 6-hour storage resource sized to the nameplate load is likely to
be sufficient to guard against curtailment risk to the level required by the load customer. Is a
battery double or quadruple that size required? The answers to these questions cannot be known
or even estimated without at least general guidance on the circumstances under which
curtailment will be triggered.

                                                       7
 storage, and load resources, our development choices depend heavily on the level of curtailment

risk predicted by the transmission services tariff terms. As Levitt explains, “a financial model

supporting a co-location investment would need assumptions regarding expected curtailment

hours, maximum event duration, seasonal concentration, event time, and whether curtailment is

tied to conditions affecting the specific delivery path or to broader PJM system conditions.”15

While developers do not need certainty with respect to each of these variables, they need

sufficient, general parameters of a service to make reasonable assumptions and assign informed

probabilities. The vague curtailment language set forth by PJM in its proposed Tariff is so open-

ended that it does not provide a basis for any particular assumptions, and so is not adequate to

support investment in co-located generation, energy storage, demand response, and other

resources to support transmission customers. The Commission’s directive to PJM to indicate

relative curtailment order is helpful, but it does not ensure that PJM will bound curtailment in a

manner necessary to ameliorate the open-ended commercial risk that its original tariff proposal

would establish. While PJM asserts in its reply brief dated April 24, 2026, that “...all generating

resource that are available ...will be utilized to serve the Interim NITS customer,” that

commitment does not appear in its Tariff language.

         And while it is true that “even specifiable practices that significantly affect rates need not

be included if they are clearly implied by the tariff’s express terms,”16 in this case neither PJM

nor the Commission has pointed to any express tariff terms that imply when and how curtailment

may occur. The Commission’s Order appropriately requires PJM to spell out curtailment priority

of both new and existing transmission services. But if curtailment priority of the new services is




15
     Id. at 4-5.
16
     Hecate Energy Greene County 3 LLC v. FERC, 72 F.4th 1307, 1314 (D.C. Cir. 2023).

                                                       8
 not equal to existing services or nested within them, the tariff may not even imply the

circumstances when curtailment may occur. The Commission’s should therefore clarify that, in

addition to providing curtailment order, PJM’s tariff must at minimum set forth general reliability

principles and circumstances when curtailment may occur so that it can implement these

principles and provide greater detail on the circumstances in its manuals.

          As Levitt persuasively argues, the most efficient approach would be to provide a clear

and precise curtailment directive in the tariff.17 But even general tariff language providing

guidance to be implemented more precisely in a manual would be a significant improvement

upon the manifestly open-ended approach taken by PJM. Such a directive would be consistent

with the level of specificity set forth for non-firm point-to-point transmission service, where the

tariff provides the following general direction regarding when curtailments for reliability or

economic reasons may occur:

                  The Transmission Provider reserves the right to Curtail, in whole or in part, Non-

                  Firm Point-To-Point Transmission Service provided under the Tariff for reliability

                  reasons when an emergency or other unforeseen condition threatens to impair or

                  degrade the reliability of the Transmission System or the systems directly and

                  indirectly interconnected with Transmission Provider's Transmission System. . . .

                  The Transmission Provider reserves the right to Interrupt, in whole or in part,

                  Non-Firm Point-To-Point Transmission Service provided under the Tariff for

                  economic reasons in order to accommodate (1) a request for Firm Transmission

                  Service, (2) a request for Non-Firm Point-To-Point Transmission Service of

                  greater duration, (3) a request for Non-Firm Point-To-Point Transmission Service



17
     See Levitt Affidavit.

                                                       9
                  of equal duration with a higher price, or (4) transmission service for Network

                 Customers from non-designated resources.18

          Notably, the point-to-point curtailment language in the tariff includes both a relative

priority order of curtailment and a description of the general reliability circumstances that trigger

when the service may be curtailed, thus providing a bound on how much curtailment could be

anticipated based on a range of potential system conditions. To satisfy the rule of reason, the

Commission must require PJM to provide at least this same level of specificity regarding the

circumstances pursuant to which the new transmission services may be curtailed.

          PJM could satisfy such a requirement by, for example, describing in its tariff the potential

reliability trigger. For instance, the tariff could allow for reliability-based curtailment when (1)

an emergency or other unforeseen condition threatens to impair or degrade the reliability of the

Transmission System or the systems directly and indirectly interconnected with Transmission

Provider’s Transmission System, as evaluated consistent with NERC reliability standards, or (2)

when no generating resource is available (i.e., not on outage or otherwise unable to be brought

on-line in a timely manner) to serve the customer. Under the rubric of this broad framework,

PJM could then set forth the specific curtailment triggers in its manuals. For example, as Levitt

explains, PJM should set forth specific resource adequacy and transmission security curtailment

triggers (including both pre- and post-contingency actions), so as to support commercial

investments and reliable system operations.19

          Providing this basic (or even a much more detailed) set of curtailment guidelines in the

tariff would not compromise PJM’s ability to preserve system reliability in varying operating




18
     PJM, Intra-PJM Tariffs, OATT, § II.14.7 Curtailment or Interruption of Service.
19
     Levitt Affidavit at 8-11.

                                                       10
 conditions, and is in fact necessary to ensure the service terms are just and reasonable and not

unduly discriminatory. Rather, as set forth in Levitt’s affidavit, greater detail from PJM would

enhance orderly system operations. Providing at least a general description of curtailment

triggers in the tariff will enhance reliability by supporting greater use of non-firm NITS and

contract demand transmission services. In fact, based on our commercial experiences as long-

standing developers of co-located load, generation, and storage resources, at least this level of

certainty is necessary for a material number of projects to use these services. By their nature,

these services each give PJM a greater set of curtailment options than were the customers to

instead take NITS. In contrast, failure to provide even the general circumstances when

curtailment may occur is not just and reasonable because it will not support investments that

avoid costly and inefficient transmission system buildout. This was the very basis of the

Commission’s co-location order.20 Additionally, leaving curtailment decisions unbounded and at

the complete discretion of PJM risks introducing the prospect of discriminatory treatment of

similarly situated transmission customers. Without even general curtailment conditions, PJM

need not work to call curtailment consistently across customers or time based on verifiable

reliability conditions. The prospect of differential treatment will further undermine customer

interest in these services and can introduce undue discrimination in the practical application of




20
  See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 160 (Dec. 2025) (“December Co-
Location Order”) (highlighting the potential avoidance of transmission system costs as a
principal benefit of the new transmission services).

                                                     11
 the tariff.21 These risks can be resolved by including “a standard set of procedures as part of the

OATT.”22

       Clarification about the need for some general guidelines on curtailment trigger, beyond

just that which may but need not necessarily be implied by curtailment priority order, is

necessary to achieve the Commission’s objectives.

III.   The Commission Should Clarify that PJM Must Allow Load Taking Interim NITS to
       Rely on Any Resource Not Obligated to Deliver to PJM or Another Entity

       The Commission’s Order addresses the question whether an Interim NITS customer may

access a Co-Located Generator during curtailments (i.e., the transmission customer’s curtailment

obligation is reduced according to the output of its Co-Located Generator). It finds that “it is just

and reasonable to prohibit the Eligible Customer taking Interim NITS on behalf of Co-Located

Load from drawing energy from the Co-Located Generator when the Eligible Customer is

curtailed, if the Co-Located Generator is a capacity resource.”23 At the same time, however, the

Commission identifies two specific circumstances where “such a restriction would not be

applicable”24: (1) “if the associated Co-Located Generator does not yet have any interconnection

service or has only provisional interconnection service”; or (2) “if the associated Co-Located

Generator is seeking capacity resource status, but [has] not yet obtained such status.”25



21
   E.ON Climate & Renewables N. Am., LLC, 137 FERC ¶ 61,076, at P38 (2011) (“The
Commission would find any policy that creates opportunities for such discriminatory behavior to
be unacceptable”).
22
   Standardization of Generator Interconnection Agreements and Procedures, Order No. 2003,
104 FERC ¶ 61,103, at P 11 (2003), order on reh'g, Order No. 2003-A, 106 FERC ¶ 61,220,
order on reh'g, Order No. 2003-B, 109 FERC ¶ 61,287 (2004), order on reh'g, Order No. 2003-C,
111 FERC ¶ 61,401 (2005), aff'd sub nom. Nat'l Ass'n of Regulatory Util. Comm'rs v. FERC, 475
F.3d 1277 (D.C. Cir. 2007) (“A standard set of procedures as part of the OATT . . . will minimize
opportunities for undue discrimination”).
23
   Order at P 576.
24
   Id.
25
   Id.

                                                     12
           The reasonable implication of these findings is that a co-located resource may be relied

upon where it is not a Generation Capacity Resource under the PJM tariff or is not otherwise

obligated to deliver its services to PJM or another entity apart from the relevant transmission

customer taking Interim NITS. Eolian agrees that it is reasonable to bar resources from

delivering solely to the Interim NITS customer when they are obligated to serve Network Load.26

However, clarification is needed to confirm that all resources not obligated to deliver to PJM or

another entity are eligible to support Interim NITS customers, because the Commission

explicitly requires tariff modification only with regard to the specific circumstances it

discusses27—leaving out additional circumstances for which a co-located resource could provide

capacity to its co-located load without being a Generation Capacity Resource. To more

completely effectuate the principle that the Commission is reasonably aiming at, it should make

clear that PJM must allow a transmission customer taking Interim NITS to rely on any resource

whenever it is not obligated to deliver to PJM or another entity apart from the relevant load

taking Interim NITS.

          The key challenge which the Commission’s ordering language does not necessarily

overcome is that for Interim NITS to be commercially workable, most loads must be able to rely

upon a co-located or electrically proximate resource until the load’s network upgrades are

completed. Where the load is developed in conjunction with a new generation resource, the

load’s network upgrades may not be completed on the same timeline as network upgrades

required to interconnect the storage or generation capacity resource. If the interconnection of

non-provisional CIRs proceeds faster than that of firm service to load, the Interim NITS




26
     Id. (“capacity resources have an obligation to serve Network Load”).
27
     Id.

                                                      13
 customer will nonetheless still need to rely on the co-located generator. For many, if not most,

large load customers, the prospect of curtailment without access to a co-located generator or

storage resource to help avoid outage is not commercially tenable. Such large load customers are

unlikely to invest, directly or through offtake agreements, in co-located or electrically proximate

generation if they cannot rely on such generation before network upgrades are completed and

NITS is provided. As a result, the very services that the Commission has found are necessary are

likely to go underutilized, substantially undermining the policy objectives that the Commission is

seeking.28 Put simply, if transmission customers are not given tools to control their own

curtailment risk when relying on Interim NITS, the service will not facilitate more timely access

to the transmission system.

       But this challenge is addressable through clarification of the Commission’s language and

through PJM’s development of new interconnection service options pursuant to the

Commission’s June 18 large load show cause order.29 While the Commission offers only two

specific examples of cases where the Interim NITS customer may rely on generation resources,

there is a broader range of circumstances where co-located or electrically proximate generation

should be able to be relied upon. For example, PJM offers Energy Resource Interconnection

Service, pursuant to which resources may obtain interconnection rights that do not grant them

Generation Capacity Resource status, or otherwise obligate them to deliver to PJM.30 PJM may



28
   See, e.g., December Co-Location Order at P 201 (finding “that this new interim, non-firm
transmission service will facilitate the timely provision of transmission service to Eligible
Customers taking transmission service on behalf of Co-Located Loads”).
29
   See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 195 FERC ¶ 61,211, at PP 95-101 (2026) (preliminarily
finding that PJM must provide new generator interconnection study procedures and services to
prevent “unnecessary interconnection delays” and “unnecessary delays and costs on transmission
customers”).
30
   See, e.g., PJM Manual 14A, at section 5 (2026) (explaining how PJM offers Energy Resource
interconnection service in addition to Capacity Resource interconnection service).

                                                    14
 develop future interconnection pathways, such as generator interconnection mechanisms in

response to the Commission’s June 18 show cause order,31 which either do not vest a resource

with Generation Capacity Resource status or else facilitate the delay in such status pending an

interim period where the resource is dedicated to the load with which it is paired. In addition,

transmission customers taking Interim NITS may seek to rely on behind-the-meter resources.

Where these resources are not used to enable the associated load to offer into the capacity market

as demand response, their capacity is not committed to PJM. The Commission’s Order expressly

extends eligibility for the new transmission services to “Eligible Customers taking transmission

service on behalf of load with BTMG” because such customers “are willing and able to limit

their energy withdrawals from the transmission system under certain conditions.”32 This

conclusion would make little sense were such customers unable to rely on their behind-the-meter

generation to support the load when Interim NITS is curtailed.

         In the event that the Commission intended to limit load to relying on co-located

generators under only the explicitly named circumstances, it should reverse that position on

rehearing. It would be unjust and unreasonable to bar Interim NITS from relying on non-capacity

resources. This is true both because workable commercial arrangements necessary to support

Interim NITS rely on the ability of transmission customers to rely on non-capacity resources to

prevent curtailment, and because Commission precedent dictates that resources should be

permitted to offer the services that they are technically capable of providing.

          Further, it would not be just and reasonable and would be unduly discriminatory to

restrict the use of such resources to prevent curtailment when such use would be consistent with




31
     See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 195 FERC ¶ 61,211, at PP 95-101 (2026).
32
     Order at P 91.

                                                    15
 their reliability obligations and reliable system operations. While the Commission reasonably

rests its prohibition of reliance on capacity resources upon the determination that “capacity

resources have an obligation to serve Network Load,”33 this logic does not extend to prohibiting

reliance on resources that are not obligated to offer into the capacity market, or that do not clear

the market to take on a capacity commitment where such resources have not otherwise

committed themselves to deliver to another entity. Commission precedent supports the

proposition that it is unjust and unreasonable for RTOs to foreclose the ability of resources to sell

services where they are technically capable of providing them.34 Just as barriers to wholesale

market participation of energy storage resources reduces market competition and thereby

contribute to unjust and unreasonable rates, barriers to the use of resources technically capable of

supporting Interim NITS customers will limit the use of that service below efficient levels and

thereby render rates unjust and unreasonable. Moreover, barring use of generation, storage, or

other resources to meet the demand of Interim NITS customers during a curtailment event when

such resources are—like the resources in the specific circumstances identified by the

Commission—technically capable of providing service to Interim NITS customers and free from

Network Load capacity service obligations, would constitute undue discrimination.35

 6   PJM’s recently approved proposal features unbounded uncertainty in the curtailment risk for

10   large load curtailment will be called.5 The upper limit of potential curtailments is therefore

20   viewpoint of prospective large-load customers, understanding curtailment triggers and the range

22   service curtailed only during defined emergency conditions and one curtailed based on broad

25   supporting a co-location investment will need assumptions regarding expected curtailment hours,

  1            IV.C.      Principles for Curtailment Triggers: Preserving Reliability
 2                       While Avoiding Excess Mandatory Curtailment
 3   We outline potential principles for curtailment triggers to maintain reliability and meet the
 4   Commission’s other objectives, including maximizing the benefits of non-firm transmission
 5   services. Triggers apply to two categories of reliability: (1) resource adequacy (ensuring
 6   sufficient supply) and (2) transmission security (keeping power flows within line limits). The
 7   impact these triggers are likely to have on the durability and adoption of the transmission service,
 8   described below, strongly indicates that these provisions materially affect rates, charges, and
 9   terms of these transmission services.

10   In the first instance, triggers need to be able to maintain reliability so that the co-location
11   arrangement has a net zero impact on resource adequacy and on transmission security. Second,
12   they should feature comparable treatment to similarly situated participants. Third, they should be
13   reasonably well specified so that participants can assess curtailment risk without unnecessary
14   uncertainty. Fourth, they should not require more curtailment than necessary for meeting the
15   other principles.

16   In general, these principles can be adhered to by mandating net withdrawal reductions only after
17   ordinary economic actions have been exhausted, with such mandates grouped together with other
18   comparable curtailments. Indeed, PJM themselves have stated this principle, stating that: “…all
19   generating resources that are available (i.e., not on outage or otherwise unable to be brought on-
20   line in a timely manner) will be utilized to serve the Interim NITS customer. The Interim NITS
21   customer would only be curtailed after these actions are taken and if the system is in an
22   unreliable state due to transmission system violations or capacity/reserve shortages.”16 To avoid
23   unnecessary uncertainty in curtailment volumes that significantly impacts commercial viability
24   of the non-firm large load transmission services, PJM need only file this principle in its Tariff.

  1                                  IV.C.1.a. Resource Adequacy Triggers

 2   An RTO or other grid operator is “resource adequate” when it has sufficient generation to serve
 3   load except under the most severe operating conditions. If a system does not satisfy resource
 4   adequacy criteria, operators may need to rely on excessive curtailments of firm load (rotating
 5   brownouts) to keep supply and demand in balance. For a paired generator and load arrangement,
 6   the fundamental resource adequacy curtailment trigger is a systemwide shortage in maintaining
 7   the supply-demand balance.

 8   Such shortages are commonly identified through a NERC-defined energy emergency alert
 9   (EEA).17 EEA Level 1 indicates that all available generation is in use; EEA Level 2 indicates that
10   load management procedures are in effect; and EEA Level 3 indicates that firm load interruption,
11   i.e., a rolling brownout, is imminent or already underway. Comparable emergency actions could
12   occur after the issuance of EEA Level 1 (prior to pre-emergency DR, with among the largest
13   curtailment exposure), during the dispatch of pre-emergency DR (prior to EEA Level 2), or
14   during PJM Emergency Procedures Step 2 (which includes issuance of EEA Level 2 and
15   simultaneous dispatch of emergency DR, the least frequent trigger that would meet definitional
16   reliability need and maximize commercial viability).18

17   This choice of trigger would have significant impacts on curtailment volumes: over the last 24
18   months, PJM has had zero EEA 3 events, two emergency demand response deployment events
19   (amounting to EEA 2 events) of 4 and 7.5 hours, and twenty-two pre-emergency demand
20   response deployment events lasting between 4.5 and 10 hours, with a median of 7.5 hours
21   duration.19 This directional trend in curtailment frequency and duration of the EEA levels is a
22   feature of their design, but the absolute value may change as supply conditions continue to
23   tighten, while weather may revert to the mean relative to the unusually high maximum
24   temperatures in PJM during the 2025 and 2026 summers.

25   Accordingly, to remain consistent with NERC definitions surrounding emergency procedures,
26   the resource adequacy triggers for serving non-firm load (or net grid withdrawals) would occur at

16                                    IV.C.1.b. Transmission Security Triggers

17   Transmission security is required to keep power flows within the operating limits of transmission
18   facilities and maintain other reliability parameters, such as voltage and stability, within
19   acceptable bounds. Because grid conditions can change instantly, transmission facilities must
20   remain within their limits even after a single contingency, such as the loss of a generating unit or
21   transmission line. For transmission security, we outline two possible categories of triggers: 1)
22   pre-contingency actions, such as operator-directed dispatch and curtailment, and 2) post-
23   contingency actions, made available by automated remedial action schemes (RAS). To preserve
24   transmission security, a load with co-located generation (or paired generation in an electrically-
25   equivalent location) must reduce net grid withdrawals to zero when the grid operator (or an
26   automated RAS) determines that doing so is necessary.20

  1   For transmission security events, PJM can determine the need for curtailment through Security
 2   Constrained Economic Dispatch (SCED), Security Constrained Unit Commitment (SCUC), or
 3   other operational planning tools. Because reducing net withdrawals generally requires curtailing
 4   high-value load, the efficient approach is to treat that curtailment as a high-cost reliability action
 5   and use it only after ordinary economic alternatives, including generator redispatch, have been
 6   exhausted. This can be achieved by configuring the load as a dispatchable asset with a high
 7   willingness to pay reflected in a bid price at some cap (such as $2,000/MWh, the offer cap for
 8   setting price as a generator, or $3,700/MWh, the bid cap for price-sensitive demand in the PJM
 9   day-ahead market).21

10   A SCED-based approach would likely set nodal market clearing prices for energy at the bid price
11   during curtailment. A SCUC-based approach may be less direct, especially because it can
12   include other values such as shut-down cost and no-load cost that would not be reflected in
13   prices even after being dispatched to reduce net withdrawals. Either way, the dispatch signal
14   coming from the PJM market engine can serve as the mandatory directive to reduce non-firm
15   load or net withdrawals at a co-location arrangement. The ability to bid at the price cap serves to
16   meet the principle of exhausting economic actions prior to relying on the withdrawal reduction to
17   maintain transmission security, thereby avoiding inefficient curtailment when not strictly needed.

18   This approach has the virtue of using the same mechanism by which co-location arrangements
19   can voluntarily reduce net withdrawals economically in response to market prices. This would be
20   expected when the marginal cost of the co-located generation is lower than market prices, or
21   when the site has been enabled with low-cost load flexibility.

22   For cases where SCED dispatch does not meet the instantaneous reliability needs, RASs are
23   useful to enable the automated reduction of net load (from the paired load and associated
24   generation) immediately upon appearance of certain reliability threshold conditions. These
25   conditions typically involve a contingency, such as the sudden loss of an internal generating unit
26   or a nearby transmission line. RAS is a well-established technology and can be relied upon for
27   ensuring transmission security if it conforms with reliability guidelines, such as those published

10   would require no curtailments during that entire period (unless there were an unexpected second
11   transmission contingency were to actually occur, which is very unlikely). The duration and
12   frequency of withdrawal reductions therefore are much greater for operator-initiated dispatch
13   than for RAS-based curtailments. RAS use thus supports commercial feasibility, where
14   appropriate to grid conditions and the capabilities of a co-location arrangement. RAS also allows
15   for the full utilization of transmission capability by offering automated curtailments in response
16   to a transmission contingency, whereas operator-initiated dispatch requires holding back
